content: A spider bite, medically referred to as arachnidism, occurs when a spider injects venom into the skin. Most spider bites are not medically significant and result in mild symptoms localized to the bite area. For a spider bite to cause significant effects, substantial envenomation is required. Bites from widow spiders involve a neurotoxic venom that can lead to a condition called latrodectism. Symptoms of latrodectism may include localized pain, which can radiate to the chest and abdomen, sweating, muscle cramps, and vomiting. In contrast, bites from recluse spiders can cause loxoscelism, characterized by local necrosis of the skin and systemic effects such as hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells). Additional symptoms may include headaches, vomiting, and mild fever. Other spiders capable of causing significant bites include the Australian funnel-web spiders, South American wandering spiders, and hobo spiders. Preventive measures against spider bites include reducing clutter in living spaces and using pesticides. Most spider bites are managed with supportive care, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen for pain and antihistamines for itching. Severe pain may require opioids. Antivenom is available for black widow spider bites, but its use is limited in the United States due to the risk of anaphylaxis. Antivenom for funnel-web spider bites has been shown to improve outcomes. In cases of recluse spider bites, surgical intervention may be necessary to repair necrotic skin damage, though most bites heal without medical intervention. Spider bites are often overdiagnosed or misdiagnosed. Historically, many conditions were incorrectly attributed to spider bites. For example, in the Middle Ages, a condition called tarantism, characterized by wild dancing, was believed to result from spider bites. While necrosis has been associated with bites from several spider species, strong evidence supports this only for recluse spiders. Not all spider bites involve venom injection. Dry bites, which do not deliver venom, typically cause pain lasting 5 to 60 minutes. In contrast, envenomating bites can cause pain lasting over 24 hours. Bleeding may also occur at the bite site. A study in Australia found that only 6% of spider bites caused significant effects, with most of these being redback spider bites that resulted in pain lasting more than 24 hours. Activation of the sympathetic nervous system from envenomation can lead to symptoms such as sweating, high blood pressure, and goosebumps. Most recluse spider bites are minor, but a small percentage can result in necrotic skin lesions, which heal slowly over months but usually resolve completely. Rarely, systemic symptoms such as profound anemia or fatalities may occur. Spiders do not feed on humans, and bites typically occur as a defensive response to unintentional contact or trapping of the spider. Most spiders have fangs too small to penetrate human skin, and bites from larger species are usually not medically significant. Medically important spider venoms may contain necrotic agents, neurotoxins, and pharmacologically active compounds like serotonin. Globally, only the venoms of widow and recluse spiders have significant effects on humans. Fatalities from widow and recluse spider bites are rare, unlike envenomation from snakes or scorpions. However, isolated spider families, such as the Brazilian wandering spider and the Australian funnel-web spider, possess lethal neurotoxic venom. Despite this, deaths are rare due to limited human contact and the availability of antivenom. Spider venom can be neurotoxic, affecting the nervous system, or necrotic, damaging tissues around the bite. Widow spider venom can cause rare complications such as heart muscle damage, which may lead to death. Funnel-web spider venom can result in pulmonary edema, a dangerous accumulation of fluid in the lungs. Recluse and South African sand spider venoms are necrotic and may cause severe hemolysis. Diagnosing spider bites can be challenging, as many reported cases are misattributed to spiders. Serious symptoms from neurotoxic envenomation typically arise within hours. Some wounds thought to be spider bites are actually infections, such as those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Many conditions, both infectious and non-infectious, can mimic spider bites, and these are often more common causes of necrotic wounds. Most spider bites are harmless and do not require specific treatment. Treatment depends on the type of spider, so capturing the spider for identification can be helpful. Basic wound care includes washing the area with soap and water and applying ice to reduce inflammation. Analgesics and antihistamines may be used, but antibiotics are not recommended unless a bacterial infection is present. For black widow envenomation, treatment focuses on managing pain and nausea. Medical attention should be sought for bites from widow spiders, Australian funnel-web spiders, or Brazilian wandering spiders, as these can develop into medical emergencies. Antivenom is available for severe widow and funnel-web envenomation. In cases of necrosis, recluse spider bites are usually self-limiting and heal without medical intervention. Recommendations to minimize damage include elevating and immobilizing the affected limb and applying ice. Local wound care and tetanus prophylaxis are standard. There is no established treatment for extensive necrosis, and surgical intervention is generally ineffective and may worsen outcomes. Dapsone, an antibiotic, is sometimes used in the United States and Brazil for necrosis, but its efficacy is debated. Antivenom may be indicated for severe spider bites, particularly those involving neurotoxic venoms. Effective antivenoms exist for Latrodectus (widow spiders), Atrax (funnel-web spiders), and Phoneutria (wandering spiders). In the United States, antivenom is administered intravenously but is rarely used due to the risk of anaphylaxis. In Australia, intramuscular antivenom use has declined. Antivenom for recluse spider bites is available in South America and shows promise, but its effectiveness may be limited if administered more than 24 hours after the bite. Estimating the prevalence of spider bites is difficult, as spider involvement is often unconfirmed. Verified bites, where the spider is identified by an expert, are more reliable for study. Misdiagnosis is common, and many conditions mistaken for spider bites are more likely to cause necrotic wounds. In Africa, several Latrodectus species (button spiders) are present, and the six-eyed sand spider may cause skin necrosis. In Australia, redback spider bites number a few thousand annually, with declining antivenom use. Funnel-web spider bites are less common, with 30–40 cases per year, 10% of which require intervention. In Europe, spider bites are rare, with 10–100 cases per million people annually. Epidemics of latrodectism from the European black widow have been documented, with up to 150 bites per year. In North America, the most concerning spiders are the brown recluse and black widow. Brown recluse bites are primarily reported in the southern and central United States, with very rare occurrences outside this region. In South America, Brazil records thousands of spider bites annually, with Loxosceles species responsible for most cases. Bites from Phoneutria (Brazilian wandering spiders) are also common but usually mild. Historically, remedies for spider bites included applying tobacco juice to the skin and, in the case of tarantism, engaging in wild dancing and music. An antivenom for wolf spiders was developed in Brazil but later abandoned, as wolf spiders were found not to cause illness.
